entities.summary:
Choricius of Gaza (fl. early to mid-6th century CE) emerged as a preeminent Greek Sophist and rhetorician, a central figure within the renowned School of Gaza during the twilight of Late Antiquity. Flourishing in an era marked by the consolidation of the early Byzantine Empire and the vibrant intellectual crosscurrents between Hellenic tradition and nascent Christian scholarship, Choricius's significance lies in his masterful articulation of classical rhetorical forms and his vivid documentation of the social, political, and cultural life of a crucial provincial city. As a student of the celebrated rhetorician Procopius of Gaza, Choricius inherited and further developed a sophisticated oratorical style, making him a key exemplar of the intellectual vitality that persisted in the eastern Roman world.

His corpus, largely preserved through a Byzantine manuscript tradition, comprises an impressive array of panegyrics, declamations, and epideictic orations. Notably, his *Laudatory Oration to Marcian* and *Declamations* offer invaluable insights into the ceremonial functions of rhetoric, the intricate patronage networks of the time, and the pedagogical practices of the Gaza school. Choricius's works frequently address imperial officials, local dignitaries, and public occasions, showcasing his skill in encomiastic praise and his engagement with contemporary civic life. He rigorously adhered to the stylistic principles of the Second Sophistic, employing elaborate figures of speech, rhythmic prose, and an encyclopedic knowledge of classical mythology and history to captivate his audiences.
